newsitem.title: USA: Sterling Q3 driven by factoring, mortgages.
newsitem.headline: Sterling Q3 driven by factoring, mortgages.

text.p: Sterling Bancorp, which reported a 45 percent rise in third-quarter net income from a year ago, is benefitting from dramatic growth in its factoring business and higher volumes in its mortgage business, president John Millman said in a telephone interview.
The higher volumes in morgages reflect the acquisition of a mortgage marketing company earlier this year, he said.
"We're very excited at what's going on at this company," Millman said. "There have been 13 consecutive quarters of more than 20 percent earnings growth."
"Factoring is a business that is growing very dramatically," Millman said. He said commissions in factoring year-to-date have nearly doubled to $622,000 from a year ago.

Although the company has been in factoring for 45 years, the specialty lending area languished under a previous management. The current team headed by chairman and chief executive Louis Cappelli has re-emphasized the area.
Asked about risks in factoring, Millman said they can be managed with credit insurance and the right credit culture. Retailers use factoring services to finance inventories.

Sterling Bancorp is a $825-million asset holding company for Sterling National Bank & Trust Co and several financial services units. Earler Monday, Sterling Bancorp said net income for the third quarter rose $2.2 million, or $0.30 per share, from $1.5 million, or $0.23 per share, a year ago. That represented a 45 percent increase in net income.

Net interest income for the third quarter of 1996 increased 14 percent to $9.9 million from $8.7 million a year ago. Non-interest income rose 88 percent to $3.1 million for the third quarter of 1996, versus $1.7 million last year, driven by the factoring and mortgage banking businesses.

Millman said the high margin lending areas such as dealer finance are growing at a much faster rate than the commercial banking core business. But he said the recent bank consolidations have left the bank considerable room to grow its lending business. He noted the company specializes in the lower end of the middle market, targeting businesses which borrow between $500,000 and $10 million.
Asked about possible future acquisitions, Millman responded, "we're always looking but it appears right now that there may be more opportunities in the non-bank financial service area."
